operationalization: Measure optical resolution, eye morphology states, and ecological performance across extant crustacean and arthropod clades, combined with biophysical optical models (such as Nilsson-Pelger steps), to test whether a continuous path of monotonically increasing visual performance exists and is represented across extant diversity.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoBank
candidate_datasets.role: Morphological character matrices of arthropod and vertebrate ocular structures across extant and fossil taxa

candidate_datasets.name: Animal Diversity Web
candidate_datasets.role: Comparative anatomical and ecological descriptions across crustacean and arthropod taxa

obstacles: Showing that graded optical states exist across living collateral relatives and are optically advantageous in simulations does not directly measure historical selection coefficients in extinct ancestors.
rationale: Comparative morphological datasets and optical physics models can directly test whether a continuous, monotonically improving sequence of eye morphologies exists across arthropods and vertebrates. However, because this is a historical mechanism claim, existing comparative data can only confirm the existence of graded functional intermediates and biophysical plausibility, rendering it partially resolvable.

operationalization: Attempt to identify any biological organ across all organisms for which every conceivable sequence of slight, viable mutational or morphological intermediates can be proven impossible.
obstacles: Proving a universal negative ('could not possibly have been formed') across all theoretical mutational and selective pathways is logically and empirically intractable with finite datasets.
Part of the claim states a methodological falsification condition for the theory rather than a bounded empirical relationship.
rationale: This claim combines a meta-theoretical falsification criterion with an unbounded universal negative across all organs of all organisms. Because no dataset can exhaustively prove that an organ could not possibly have evolved via any sequence of slight steps, the claim cannot be empirically resolved by data analysis.

operationalization: Perform ancestral state reconstruction of gas-filled pharyngeal organs (paired ventral lungs vs. dorsal hydrostatic swimbladders) on a time-calibrated vertebrate phylogeny integrating developmental gene expression and fossil osteichthyan data; the claim is confirmed if a dorsal flotation swimbladder is reconstructed as ancestral to lungs, and refuted if paired respiratory lungs arose first and gave rise to swimbladders.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoBank
candidate_datasets.role: Vertebrate and osteichthyan morphological character matrices for ancestral state reconstruction

candidate_datasets.name: Open Tree of Life
candidate_datasets.role: Synthetic vertebrate phylogeny for mapping the distribution of lungs and swimbladders across jawed fishes and tetrapods

candidate_datasets.name: Bgee
candidate_datasets.role: Comparative gene expression data across vertebrate organs to establish homology between lungs and swimbladders

obstacles: Soft-tissue gas bladders rarely fossilize directly, requiring reliance on extant phylogenetic bracketing (Polypterus, lungfishes, coelacanths, actinopterygians) and osteological correlates.
rationale: Comparative vertebrate anatomy and phylogenetic bracketing map cleanly onto a testable ancestral state reconstruction problem. Because extant basal actinopterygians (such as bichirs) and basal sarcopterygians possess paired ventral respiratory lungs while dorsal hydrostatic swimbladders are restricted to more derived neopterygians, existing phylogenetic and anatomical datasets directly refute Darwin's polarity (showing lungs were ancestral to swimbladders rather than vice versa).

operationalization: Test for independent evolutionary origins (homoplasy) of electric organs in fishes and bioluminescence in insects on molecular phylogenies, and test for positive selection ($d_N/d_S > 1$) or parallel regulatory evolution in the underlying homologous genes (e.g., voltage-gated sodium channels $scn4aa$) across convergent lineages.

candidate_datasets.name: Open Tree of Life
candidate_datasets.role: Phylogenetic trees of vertebrates and insects to test independent origins of electric organs and bioluminescence

candidate_datasets.name: NCBI GenBank
candidate_datasets.role: Coding sequences of ion channel and muscle/electric organ genes across Gymnotiformes, Mormyridae, Torpediniformes, Rajiformes, and Siluriformes

candidate_datasets.name: Ensembl
candidate_datasets.role: Comparative vertebrate genomes and gene trees for testing parallel molecular evolution in electric fishes

obstacles: Distinguishing adaptive natural selection from neutral drift at specific amino acid sites requires sufficient taxon sampling across convergent and non-convergent sister clades.
rationale: This claim can be directly operationalized using phylogenetic ancestral state reconstruction to demonstrate independent origins (convergence) and comparative genomic tests of positive and parallel selection in the underlying myogenic precursor genes. Openly available sequence and tree data for electric fishes (mormyrids, gymnotiforms, electric catfish, torpediniforms) provide a decisive test.

operationalization: Survey anatomical ontology terms across plant and animal clades and calculate the proportion of defined major organ classes that exhibit intermediate or simplified structural states in extant or fossil relatives.

candidate_datasets.name: Uberon
candidate_datasets.role: Cross-species anatomical ontology defining animal organs and their homology/structural relationships

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoBank
candidate_datasets.role: Coded morphological character states across plant and animal phylogenies

obstacles: Terms like 'rarely' and 'transitional grade' lack an objective quantitative threshold, and 'organs' can beindividuated at arbitrary granularity.
Defining a state in a collateral relative as a 'transitional grade' toward another organ can be subjective or circular.
rationale: While anatomical ontologies and phylogenetic character matrices allow systematic enumeration of organ states across taxa, Darwin's statement that it is 'rare' to find an organ without a transitional grade depends heavily on how organs and transitional grades are defined and individuated. Existing data can test specific subsets of complex organs, making it partially resolvable.

operationalization: Partition variance in multi-trait morphological character matrices (e.g., tetrapod limb osteology) into phylogenetic covariance (Pagel's $\lambda$, Blomberg's $K$, or phylogenetic mixed models) versus ecological/locomotor habit predictors; confirm if phylogenetic signal accounts for the majority of structural trait presence and topological arrangement.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoBank
candidate_datasets.role: Discrete and continuous osteological and anatomical character matrices across mammals and other tetrapods

candidate_datasets.name: Animal Diversity Web
candidate_datasets.role: Ecological habit and locomotor mode classifications for mammal and vertebrate species

candidate_datasets.name: Open Tree of Life
candidate_datasets.role: Phylogenetic topology for quantifying phylogenetic signal versus ecological adaptation

obstacles: Relative proportions of variance explained by phylogeny vs. ecology depend on whether discrete topological characters (bone presence/connectivity) or continuous morphometric dimensions (bone lengths) are analyzed.
rationale: Modern phylogenetic comparative methods (such as phylogenetic mixed models and Pagel's lambda) directly quantify the proportion of anatomical organization attributable to shared ancestry versus current ecological habit. Public morphological matrices and trait databases for mammals and other clades make this test straightforward and decisive.

operationalization: In candidate interspecific mutualisms or host-parasite systems (e.g., extrafloral nectaries, plant galls), measure lifetime reproductive fitness of individuals bearing vs. lacking the structure in the presence and absence of the partner species; the claim is refuted if a genetically encoded trait evolved in the bearer's lineage while conferring zero or negative inclusive fitness to the bearer across its evolutionary context.

candidate_datasets.name: Dryad Digital Repository
candidate_datasets.role: Published experimental datasets measuring fitness costs and benefits of mutualistic structures (e.g., extrafloral nectaries, domatia) and parasite-induced galls

obstacles: Like ch06-08, this is a universal negative across all interacting species, so confirming it across all organisms is impossible, though focal putative counterexamples can be tested.
Structures induced by parasites (extended phenotypes such as plant galls) must be distinguished from modifications encoded and selected in the host's own lineage.
rationale: As a universal negative across all species, full confirmation is impossible, but specific candidate counterexamples (such as mutualistic rewards or rattlesnake rattles) can be and have been tested using experimental fitness datasets in repositories like Dryad. Because existing data can test focal candidate cases but cannot exhaustively survey all species or historical selective environments, it is partially resolvable.

operationalization: Test for asymmetry in naturalization success, population displacement, and extinction risk between continental introductions to islands (such as New Zealand) and island-to-continent introductions, controlling for propagule pressure and human habitat disturbance.

candidate_datasets.name: Global Naturalized Alien Flora (GloNAF)
candidate_datasets.role: Global occurrences and donor/recipient regions of naturalized plant species across islands and continents

candidate_datasets.name: Global Invasive Species Database (GISD)
candidate_datasets.role: Records of invasive species impacts, origins, and recipient ecosystems worldwide

candidate_datasets.name: IUCN Red List of Threatened Species
candidate_datasets.role: Extinction and threat status of endemic island vs. continental species driven by invasive competitors and predators

obstacles: Higher invasion impact on islands is confounded by human land-use change, differential propagule pressure (trade asymmetry), and release from coevolved continental enemies rather than intrinsic competitive superiority alone.
rationale: Darwin's observable consequence—that endemic island biotas (such as New Zealand's) disproportionately yield to species introduced from larger continental regions—can be directly tested with global invasion and threat databases like GloNAF, GISD, and the IUCN Red List. While mechanistic interpretation faces confounds from propagule pressure and enemy release, the empirical pattern and directional competitive asymmetry are directly resolvable now.

operationalization: Map the phylogenetic origin of structural traits (such as open cranial sutures/fontanelles) relative to the origin of the putative co-opted function (viviparity with narrow birth-canal passage in mammals) on a time-calibrated amniote phylogeny; confirm if the trait significantly predates the functional regime in oviparous ancestors.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoBank
candidate_datasets.role: Cranial osteology and suture developmental character matrices across amniotes (synapsids, reptiles, birds, mammals)

candidate_datasets.name: Paleobiology Database
candidate_datasets.role: Fossil occurrences and temporal ranges of non-mammalian synapsids, reptiles, and early mammals

obstacles: While Darwin's specific skull-suture example can be tested phylogenetically, the broader claim that 'many modifications' arose non-adaptively from laws of growth and were later co-opted cannot be comprehensively quantified across all plants and animals.
rationale: Darwin's specific historical inference about cranial sutures (exaptation from oviparous amniote skull growth to mammalian parturition) is directly testable via phylogenetic character mapping on amniote trees, which confirms that patent neonatal cranial sutures predate mammalian viviparity. However, the broader generalization across 'many modifications' and proving that initial origins were strictly non-adaptive ('in no way advantageous') is only partially resolvable.

operationalization: Measure morphological step sizes between ancestor-descendant pairs across densely sampled microstratigraphic fossil lineages to test whether transitions approach continuous infinitesimal gradations as temporal resolution increases.

candidate_datasets.name: Paleobiology Database
candidate_datasets.role: Global fossil occurrence records illustrating sampling gaps and preserved morphological series

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoBank
candidate_datasets.role: Morphological character matrices including fossil and extant taxa

obstacles: The vast majority of all past organisms that ever lived were never fossilized, making 'if we include all those of past times' empirically inaccessible in full.

Even in high-resolution fossil sequences (e.g., marine microfossils), punctuated stasis vs. rapid cladogenesis and discrete mutations (e.g., polyploidy, homeotic shifts) complicate what counts as 'strictly true' continuity.
rationale: Darwin explicitly predicates this claim on including *all* past organisms that ever lived, the overwhelming majority of which were never preserved in the geological record. While high-resolution microfossil sequences can test gradualism in select lineages, existing fossil datasets cover a minuscule fraction of all past life, so resolving the claim as stated requires data that are largely unpreserved.

operationalization: Test for hierarchical congruence (tree-to-tree similarity and shared monophyly) between phylogenies inferred from homologous anatomical 'unity of type' characters and independent phylogenies inferred from neutral genomic sequences across organisms within major classes, regardless of ecological guild.

candidate_datasets.name: Open Tree of Life
candidate_datasets.role: Synthetic phylogenies across major taxonomic classes

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoBank
candidate_datasets.role: Anatomical homology matrices across vertebrate and invertebrate classes

candidate_datasets.name: NCBI GenBank
candidate_datasets.role: Independent molecular sequence data to test whether anatomical 'unity of type' reflects common genealogical descent

obstacles: Evaluating 'unity of type is explained by unity of descent' requires avoiding circularity by comparing morphological homology trees against independent molecular sequence trees and testing against non-genealogical null models (e.g., purely functional/ecological clustering).
rationale: While framed as an explanatory principle, it makes the clear, non-circular prediction that fundamental anatomical homologies within a class follow a nested hierarchical tree structure that matches independent genomic genealogies rather than grouping by ecological habit. Public morphological and genomic databases allow this congruence test to be run cleanly today.

operationalization: Estimate additive genetic heritability ($h^2$) and selection gradients on innate behavioral traits in wild animal populations, and compare them against transgenerational epigenetic or maternal inheritance of learned habits across generations in the absence of genetic selection.

candidate_datasets.name: Dryad Digital Repository
candidate_datasets.role: Quantitative genetic pedigree and cross-fostering datasets of behavioral traits in wild birds, mammals, and insects

candidate_datasets.name: NCBI Sequence Read Archive (SRA)
candidate_datasets.role: Genomic and methylome datasets from behavioral selection and transgenerational plasticity studies

obstacles: Direct experimental tests simultaneously partitioning genetic selection vs. transgenerational inheritance of learned habits in wild populations exist only for a small number of model behavioral systems.
Darwin's concept of 'inherited effects of habit' (Lamarckian use-inheritance) must be mapped onto modern transgenerational behavioral epigenetics or social learning to be tested.
rationale: Quantitative genetics and cross-fostering datasets in wild animals demonstrate significant additive genetic variance and natural selection on innate behaviors, while showing little evidence that learned habits become genetically fixed without selection. However, because data simultaneously measuring both mechanisms across complex natural instincts are restricted to a few model taxa, the claim is partially resolvable.

operationalization: Score complex innate behavioral repertoires (e.g., nest architecture in birds or social wasps, web building in spiders, brood care in insects) as multistate ordered characters across species phylogenies, and test whether gradual step-by-step models (Pagel's $\lambda$, ordered Markov models, or continuous Brownian/OU models) fit better than saltational jump models and whether intermediate behavioral states occur in collateral relatives.

candidate_datasets.name: Dryad Digital Repository
candidate_datasets.role: Published comparative behavioral datasets (e.g., avian nest architecture, spider web structure, hymenopteran social behavior) with matched phylogenies

candidate_datasets.name: Open Tree of Life
candidate_datasets.role: Phylogenetic trees for testing phylogenetic signal and gradual transitions in behavioral traits

obstacles: No single unified global database of standardized behavioral ethograms exists across all animals; datasets are clade-specific (e.g., birds, spiders, bees).
Extinction of basal lineages can create apparent gaps between behavioral states in extant species.
rationale: Comparative behavioral datasets for major model clades (such as bird nest building, spider web construction, and bee sociality) are openly available on Dryad and allow phylogenetic tests of behavioral gradation across collateral relatives. Because standardized behavioral trait data are only compiled for specific clades rather than all animal instincts, it is partially resolvable.

operationalization: In candidate interspecific behavioral interactions (such as aphid honeydew excretion in the presence of ants, cleaner-client fish interactions, or interspecific alarm calling), measure direct and inclusive fitness effects on the actor with and without the partner species; the claim is refuted if an evolved, non-parasitized instinct reduces or provides zero fitness benefit to the actor while solely benefiting the other species.

candidate_datasets.name: Dryad Digital Repository
candidate_datasets.role: Experimental datasets quantifying fitness costs and benefits of ant-aphid tending and other interspecific mutualisms

obstacles: As a universal negative ('no animal in the world'), it cannot be exhaustively verified across all species, though Darwin's focal case (aphids and ants) and other mutualisms can be tested.

Behaviors induced by manipulative parasites (e.g., hairworms driving crickets into water, Toxoplasma, parasitoid wasps) perform actions exclusively for the parasite's good, requiring a distinction between the actor's own evolved instincts and pathological manipulation.
rationale: Darwin's focal example (aphid honeydew excretion and ant tending) and other mutualisms have public experimental data confirming mutual fitness benefits or physiological necessity (excretion). However, the universal negative phrasing across all animals and the existence of parasite-manipulated host behaviors (which benefit only the parasite) complicate a global test, making the claim partially resolvable.

operationalization: Quantify intraspecific, inter-population variance in migratory distance, migratory bearing, and proportion of resident (non-migratory) individuals across wild bird species using GPS tracking, bird-banding recovery, and citizen-science occurrence data; confirm if significant within-species geographic variation and partial/lost migration occur.

candidate_datasets.name: Movebank
candidate_datasets.role: Individual animal tracking data showing intraspecific variation in migratory distance, direction, and residency across wild bird populations

candidate_datasets.name: eBird
candidate_datasets.role: Global spatiotemporal bird occurrence records documenting sedentary vs. migratory populations within species

candidate_datasets.name: Global Biodiversity Information Facility (GBIF)
candidate_datasets.role: Georeferenced seasonal occurrence and specimen data across species' ranges

obstacles: Observational tracking data in the wild combine genetic differences in migratory instinct with environmental plasticity, though common-garden studies (e.g., in Sylvia warblers) available in repositories separate the two.
rationale: Darwin's empirical generalization—that instincts such as bird migration vary in extent, direction, and complete loss within wild species—maps directly onto modern movement ecology datasets. Movebank and eBird provide massive, openly accessible data across hundreds of avian species confirming widespread intraspecific variation and partial migration.

operationalization: Regress flight initiation distance (FID, the distance at which an animal flees an approaching human) against island vs. mainland status, time since human colonization/persecution intensity, and body mass across bird and reptile species, controlling for phylogeny.

candidate_datasets.name: Dryad Digital Repository
candidate_datasets.role: Global comparative datasets of avian and reptilian Flight Initiation Distance (FID) across islands vs. continents and across body sizes

candidate_datasets.name: AVONET
candidate_datasets.role: Body mass, island endemicity, and morphological traits for all bird species to pair with FID datasets

obstacles: Observational FID measurements reflect both evolved genetic wariness and within-lifetime learning/habituation to benign vs. hunting human presence.
rationale: Flight Initiation Distance (FID) is a standard, widely measured metric in behavioral ecology directly operationalizing 'fear of man'. Large global comparative FID datasets published in Dryad test both island tameness (reduced FID on isolated islands with short human histories) and the positive relationship between body mass/hunting pressure and FID in birds.

operationalization: Test for narrow-sense heritability ($h^2$) of breed-defining behavioral instincts (pointing, herding, retrieving, tameness) and scan for selective sweeps at neurobehavioral loci across domestic animal breeds compared to wild progenitors, while comparing against non-genetic transgenerational effects of training.

candidate_datasets.name: NCBI Sequence Read Archive (SRA)
candidate_datasets.role: Whole-genome sequencing of dog, pigeon, chicken, and rabbit breeds and wild ancestors to detect selection signatures on behavioral genes

candidate_datasets.name: Dryad Digital Repository
candidate_datasets.role: Canine behavioral assessment (C-BARQ) and genomic association datasets across dog breeds

obstacles: Darwin attributes domestic instincts partly to inherited habit (use-inheritance) and partly to selection of chance variations; genomic and pedigree datasets strongly confirm artificial selection on genetic variation, but testing transgenerational inheritance of training across breeds is harder with existing data.
rationale: Large public canine behavioral and genomic datasets (such as C-BARQ paired with breed genotypes) directly test the high heritability and selective sweeps underlying domestic behavioral traits like herding and pointing. However, evaluating the exact historical balance between unconscious vs. methodical selection and Darwin's proposed Lamarckian 'inherited habit' component across multiple domestic species makes it partially resolvable.

operationalization: Reconstruct the ancestral state of parental care vs. facultative and obligate brood parasitism across a time-calibrated phylogeny of Cuculidae (and other avian clades with brood parasites), and test whether obligate brood parasitism evolved from nest-building ancestors via facultative conspecific/interspecific parasitism and whether parasitic eggs/chicks achieve high fledging success in host nests.

candidate_datasets.name: Open Tree of Life
candidate_datasets.role: Phylogenetic trees of Cuculidae and all birds for ancestral state reconstruction of brood parasitism

candidate_datasets.name: AVONET
candidate_datasets.role: Avian ecological and life-history data across cuckoos and other bird families

candidate_datasets.name: Dryad Digital Repository
candidate_datasets.role: Comparative datasets on avian brood parasitism evolution, facultative nest dumping, and host-parasite reproductive success

obstacles: In Cuculidae, obligate parasitism evolved three independent times from nest-building ancestors, and extant intermediate facultative parasites (such as Coccyzus) are fewer than fully nest-building or obligate clades.
rationale: Phylogenetic comparative datasets of the cuckoo family (Cuculidae) and all birds are publicly available and directly test whether obligate brood parasitism evolved from nest-building ancestors and whether facultative brood parasitism exists as a viable intermediate strategy. Existing phylogenetic and behavioral ecology data resolve this historical pathway well.

operationalization: Reconstruct the evolutionary transitions among free-living predation/brood raiding, temporary social parasitism, facultative dulosis (as in Formica sanguinea), and obligate dulosis (as in Polyergus) on a molecular phylogeny of Formicidae, testing Darwin's predation-first pathway against the rival temporary-social-parasitism or territorial-brood-raiding pathways.

candidate_datasets.name: AntWeb
candidate_datasets.role: Taxonomic, distribution, and natural history data for slave-making and free-living ant species

candidate_datasets.name: Open Tree of Life
candidate_datasets.role: Phylogenetic relationships within Formicinae and Myrmicinae

candidate_datasets.name: Dryad Digital Repository

obstacles: Phylogenetic reconstructions in Formicinae often cannot cleanly discriminate Darwin's 'pupae captured as food' origin from rival hypotheses (such as temporary queen social parasitism or territorial brood raiding among closely related species, per Emery's rule).
rationale: Molecular phylogenies and behavioral trait datasets of dulotic ants exist in public repositories and clearly test the progression from facultative to obligate slave-making. However, because dulotic ants almost always parasitize closely related species (Emery's rule), existing comparative data struggle to definitively separate Darwin's 'food predation' origin from temporary social parasitism or territorial brood transport, making it partially resolvable.

operationalization: Map nest and brood-cell architectural characters (single cells, irregular clusters, spherical storage pots with flat brood combs, double-sided hexagonal combs) onto a time-calibrated molecular phylogeny of corbiculate bees (Euglossini, Bombini, Meliponini, Apini) to test whether comb complexity evolved via gradual state transitions.

candidate_datasets.name: Open Tree of Life
candidate_datasets.role: Phylogeny of Apidae and the four corbiculate bee tribes (Apini, Bombini, Meliponini, Euglossini)

candidate_datasets.name: Dryad Digital Repository
candidate_datasets.role: Phylogenomic datasets and nest-architecture character matrices of corbiculate bees

obstacles: The four extant corbiculate tribes diverged tens of millions of years ago and many extinct stem Apini lineages are unpreserved, leaving only four major extant clades to reconstruct the exact sequence of architectural transitions.
rationale: Phylogenomic trees and nest-architecture character matrices for corbiculate bees (orchid bees, bumblebees, stingless bees, and honeybees) are publicly available and allow ancestral state reconstruction of comb building. While extant diversity demonstrates the functional viability of intermediate nest architectures (such as Melipona), the deep divergence among the four extant tribes limits fine-grained resolution of the exact ancestral steps.

operationalization: Analyze high-resolution 3D micro-CT scans, time-lapse recordings, and geometric measurements of honeybee comb construction from initial spherical/cylindrical wax cups to planar hexagonal walls and rhombic bases, testing whether active wax-gnawing/excavation of intersection planes (Darwin's mechanism) or thermoplastic surface-tension flow of heated wax drives hexagon formation.

candidate_datasets.name: Dryad Digital Repository
candidate_datasets.role: Published morphometric, video-tracking, and micro-CT datasets of Apis mellifera comb construction, cell geometry, and wax thermo-mechanics

candidate_datasets.name: Figshare
candidate_datasets.role: Open datasets of honeybee cell geometry, wall thickness, and construction progression

obstacles: Experimental studies show that while bees initially build cylindrical/hemispherical cups spaced equally apart, the transition to flat hexagonal walls with 120-degree angles is also strongly mediated by thermoplastic flow of wax heated by bees' bodies rather than purely mechanical excavation.
rationale: Darwin's mechanistic hypothesis about how bees construct hexagonal cells makes concrete geometric and physical predictions about initial cup spacing, wall thickness, and construction stages. Publicly available experimental datasets on Dryad and Figshare (measuring cell geometry over time, substrate gap merging, and wax thermal properties) directly test and partially revise Darwin's mechanical excavation model.

operationalization: Compare the surface-area-to-volume ratio of the three-rhombi pyramidal base (Maraldi angle $\approx 109^\circ 28'$) of Apis mellifera cells against alternative space-filling polyhedral cell terminations ( specifically the Weaire-Phelan / Tóth truncated octahedron apex with two hexagons and two rhombi) and empirical micro-CT measurements of real combs; refute 'absolute perfection' if another geometry uses strictly less wax surface area for the same volume.

candidate_datasets.name: Dryad Digital Repository
candidate_datasets.role: 3D micro-CT and geometric morphometric datasets of Apis mellifera comb cell angles, wall thicknesses, and volumes

obstacles: While mathematically a Tóth truncated-octahedron base saves ~0.35% surface area for thin walls, real comb walls have finite thickness and rounded fillets where mechanical stability and larval fit also matter.
rationale: Whether the honeybee comb geometry minimizes surface area per unit volume ('absolutely perfect in economising wax') is both mathematically and empirically resolvable. Mathematical proof (Fejes Tóth 1964, showing a two-hexagon/two-rhombus apex saves ~0.35% area over the bee's three-rhombus Maraldi apex) combined with empirical 3D comb measurements on Dryad directly resolves the claim.

operationalization: Estimate the genetic variance among colonies (queens/kings) in sterile worker morphological or behavioral phenotypes and measure the selection differential on colony reproductive output (alates/gynes/drones produced) as a function of worker traits in natural populations, combined with genomic tests of selection on worker-biased genes.

candidate_datasets.name: Dryad Digital Repository
candidate_datasets.role: Colony-level fitness, worker trait heritability, and kin-selection datasets across ants, honeybees, bumblebees, and wasps

candidate_datasets.name: NCBI Sequence Read Archive (SRA)

operationalization: Measure continuous morphometric traits (head width, mandible length, thorax length, ocellus development) across sterile workers sampled from single colonies across ant species, and test for unimodal continuous or continuous allometric distributions connecting minor and major worker morphologies within nests.

candidate_datasets.name: AntWeb

operationalization: Categorize ant species into monomorphic, continuously polymorphic (allometric gradations), and dimorphic/discrete castes (lacking intermediates), and perform ancestral state reconstruction on a time-calibrated Formicidae phylogeny to test whether discrete dimorphic castes evolve from continuously polymorphic ancestors.

candidate_datasets.name: AntWeb
candidate_datasets.role: Morphological documentation of worker caste polymorphism across ant genera

candidate_datasets.name: GlobalAnts
candidate_datasets.role: Global database of ant morphological and ecological traits including worker polymorphism across species

candidate_datasets.name: Dryad Digital Repository
candidate_datasets.role: Comparative datasets and phylogenies of worker caste evolution across Formicidae

obstacles: In some genera (e.g., Pheidole), complete dimorphism is conserved across hundreds of species, so transitions between continuous polymorphism and discrete dimorphism must be inferred across deeper subfamily nodes.
rationale: Darwin's historical inference—that discrete worker castes evolved from a continuously graduated polymorphic series by elimination of intermediates—can be directly tested via phylogenetic comparative methods on ant caste datasets. operationalization: Quantify phylogenetic signal (Pagel's $\lambda$ or Blomberg's $K$) in innate behavioral traits (e.g., nest construction type, foraging stratum, song structure) across congeneric or confamilial bird species inhabiting different biogeographic realms and climatic niches, controlling for environmental distance.

candidate_datasets.name: AVONET
candidate_datasets.role: Global avian dataset of ecological, trophic, and geographical range attributes across all bird species

candidate_datasets.name: Xeno-canto
candidate_datasets.role: Global repository of bird vocalizations across biogeographic regions to test phylogenetic conservatism of acoustic instincts

candidate_datasets.name: Dryad Digital Repository
candidate_datasets.role: Global comparative datasets of avian nest architecture, foraging behavior, and phylogeny

operationalization: Compare gamete/gonad functionality in pure parental species undergoing heterospecific crosses (measuring prezygotic pollen-pistil/sperm-egg barriers and F1 seed/zygote set) against gonad development, meiotic pairing, and gamete viability (pollen stainability, sperm motility, ovarian development) in the resulting F1 hybrids across plant and animal species pairs.

candidate_datasets.name: Dryad Digital Repository
candidate_datasets.role: Comparative datasets of prezygotic/extrinsic cross-incompatibility vs. intrinsic F1 hybrid sterility (pollen/sperm viability) across Drosophila, birds, amphibians, and angiosperm genera

candidate_datasets.name: Mouse Phenome Database
candidate_datasets.role: Reproductive organ weights, sperm counts, and fertility metrics in pure Mus species/subspecies vs. interspecific F1 hybrids

obstacles: In some crosses, F1 inviability (embryo lethality) prevents measuring F1 reproductive organ function, requiring the comparison to focus on crosses that produce viable F1 adults.
rationale: Darwin's distinction between the failure of pure, reproductively normal species to produce hybrid offspring (first-cross incompatibility/F1 inviability) and the functional impotence of the reproductive organs in viable F1 hybrids (intrinsic postzygotic hybrid sterility, e.g., meiotic failure or gametogenesis arrest) maps directly onto modern speciation genetics datasets. Extensive comparative crossing datasets on Dryad confirm these are distinct biological phenomena.

operationalization: Measure reproductive output (seed set, litter size, hatching success, offspring survival) as a function of pedigree inbreeding coefficient ($F$) versus outcrossing with distinct lines/varieties (heterosis), and compare multi-generation hybrid fertility under sib-mating/selfing versus outcrossing across plant and animal datasets.

candidate_datasets.name: Dryad Digital Repository
candidate_datasets.role: Meta-analytic and experimental datasets on inbreeding depression, heterosis, and multi-generation hybrid fertility in plants and animals

candidate_datasets.name: Mouse Phenome Database
candidate_datasets.role: Fertility and litter size records across inbred strains vs. F1/outcrossed crosses

candidate_datasets.name: Germplasm Resources Information Network (GRIN)
candidate_datasets.role: Crop germplasm evaluation records comparing selfed/inbred lines with inter-varietal crosses

obstacles: In F2 and later interspecific hybrid generations, declining fertility is driven by both inbreeding (from small sample sizes of experimental hybrids, as Darwin noted) and Dobzhansky-Muller hybrid breakdown (recombination breaking up coadapted gene complexes).
rationale: Inbreeding depression and heterosis (hybrid vigor upon crossing distinct lines or varieties) are among the most thoroughly documented phenomena in experimental biology and agriculture. Public datasets on Dryad, GRIN, and animal breeding repositories directly confirm that close inbreeding reduces fertility while outcrossing restores it, and allow partitioning inbreeding effects from recombinant hybrid breakdown.

operationalization: Use whole-genome ancestry and admixture analyses of domestic animal breeds (dogs, taurine/indicine cattle, pigs, chickens, sheep, goats) and their wild relatives to test whether domesticates descend from multiple distinct wild species or primarily from a single wild progenitor species (with minor introgression), and compare interspecific hybrid fertility in wild vs. domestic conditions.

candidate_datasets.name: NCBI Sequence Read Archive (SRA)
candidate_datasets.role: Whole-genome sequences of domestic dogs, wolves, coyotes, jackals, taurine/zebu cattle, chickens, and wild junglefowl

candidate_datasets.name: Ensembl
candidate_datasets.role: Reference genomes and variation data for domestic species and wild congeners

obstacles: Darwin's premise—that domestic dogs and other domesticates descend from several distinct wild species—has been largely overturned by modern genomics (dogs descend from grey wolves, Canis lupus), though Bos taurus x Bos indicus and Gallus gallus x Gallus sonneratii introgression provide partial tests.
rationale: Darwin's argument rests on the testable historical premise that domestic animals such as dogs descend from multiple distinct wild species whose interspecific sterility was removed by domestication. Modern population genomic datasets in NCBI SRA and Ensembl directly resolve this premise (showing single-species origins for dogs from Canis lupus, while clarifying where inter-subspecific or interspecific introgression actually occurred), allowing the claim to be evaluated directly.

operationalization: Calculate the distribution of prezygotic crossability and postzygotic F1 hybrid fertility indices across large multi-taxon compilations of interspecific crosses in plants and animals; confirm if the vast majority show reduced fertility ($< 1.0$ relative to conspecific crosses) while a non-zero fraction of recognized species pairs produce fully fertile F1 hybrids.

candidate_datasets.name: Dryad Digital Repository
candidate_datasets.role: Large comparative speciation datasets of reproductive isolation and hybrid fertility across Drosophila, birds, fishes, frogs, and angiosperms (e.g., Coyne & Orr, Moyle, Lowry, Rabosky & Matute compilations)

obstacles: Taxonomic circularity can arise if taxonomists use reproductive isolation itself to delimit species, though phylogenetic and morphological species definitions allow independent tests.
rationale: Comparative reproductive isolation datasets across thousands of plant and animal species pairs are openly archived on Dryad. These datasets directly quantify first-cross compatibility and F1 fertility, confirming both that reduced fertility is the general rule across species pairs and that fully fertile interspecific crosses occur in numerous young plant and animal radiations.

operationalization: Compute the correlation ($r$ or phylogenetic generalized least squares slope) and residual scatter between prezygotic/first-cross incompatibility (proportion of pollinations or matings failing to yield F1 zygotes/seeds) and intrinsic postzygotic F1 hybrid sterility (pollen/ovule or sperm/egg non-viability) across interspecific crosses in plants and animals.

candidate_datasets.name: Dryad Digital Repository
candidate_datasets.role: Comparative datasets measuring multiple sequential prezygotic (pollen-pistil/mating/seed-set) and postzygotic (F1 pollen/seed fertility, F1 gametogenesis) reproductive barriers across plant genera (Silene, Solanum, Mimulus, Nolana) and animal clades (Drosophila, Etheostoma, amphibians)

obstacles: Crosses that completely fail at the first-cross stage ($RI_{pre} = 1.0$) cannot be assayed for F1 hybrid sterility, truncating the upper end of the joint distribution.
rationale: Modern speciation studies routinely measure prezygotic/first-cross success and postzygotic F1 hybrid sterility as separate variables across dozens of species pairs per clade. Publicly archived datasets on Dryad allow immediate calculation of their correlation and discordant cases, directly confirming Darwin's observation that the two barriers correlate only loosely.

operationalization: Regress first-cross success and F1 hybrid fertility against phylogenetic/genetic distance ($K_s$, patristic distance, or taxonomic rank from congeneric to interfamilial) across plant and animal crossing datasets; confirm a strong positive relationship with affinity (negative relationship with divergence distance) alongside substantial variance among closely related species pairs.

candidate_datasets.name: Dryad Digital Repository
candidate_datasets.role: Comparative speciation clock datasets pairing genetic divergence/phylogenetic distance with crossability and hybrid sterility in Drosophila, birds, frogs, fishes, Lepidoptera, and angiosperms

candidate_datasets.name: Open Tree of Life
candidate_datasets.role: Taxonomic and phylogenetic relationships for species pairs in hybridization studies

obstacles: Historical 19th-century 'systematic affinity' was based on morphology rather than molecular divergence, though both morphological taxonomy and molecular divergence yield the same macro-pattern.
rationale: This claim corresponds directly to the 'speciation clock' (reproductive isolation as a function of phylogenetic divergence and taxonomic affinity), one of the best-documented empirical datasets in evolutionary biology. Openly available datasets on Dryad across plants and animals allow immediate regression of cross fertility against phylogenetic and taxonomic affinity.

operationalization: Quantify reproductive isolation asymmetry ($|RI_{A \times B} - RI_{B \times A}|$) in reciprocal interspecific crosses where both directions were tested in plants and animals, and test the prevalence and magnitude of significant directional asymmetry in seed set, fertilization, or F1 viability/fertility.

candidate_datasets.name: Dryad Digital Repository
candidate_datasets.role: Reciprocal cross datasets documenting asymmetric reproductive isolation ('Darwin's corollary to Haldane's rule') across angiosperms, Drosophila, centrarchid fishes, and amphibians

obstacles: None of significance; reciprocal cross asymmetry is directly measured in standard diallel crossing designs.
rationale: Reciprocal cross asymmetry is so well known in evolutionary genetics that Turelli and Moyle (2007) named it 'Darwin's corollary to Haldane's rule'. Large compiled datasets of reciprocal crosses in plants (pollen-style unilateral incompatibility, cytonuclear interactions) and animals are openly available in Dryad and directly confirm the claim.

operationalization: Test whether intrinsic hybrid sterility and inviability accumulate as a monotonic byproduct of divergence in allopatry (following the Dobzhansky-Muller epistatic model between independently diverging reproductive loci) versus being elevated specifically in sympatry via direct selection for sterility (reinforcement of postzygotic sterility), and identify the functional divergence of cloned hybrid sterility genes (e.g., Odysseys, Prdm9, Overdrive).

candidate_datasets.name: Dryad Digital Repository
candidate_datasets.role: Comparative datasets comparing intrinsic postzygotic hybrid sterility in allopatric vs. sympatric species pairs, and QTL/introgression maps of Dobzhansky-Muller incompatibilities

candidate_datasets.name: FlyBase
candidate_datasets.role: Genetic and molecular characterization of hybrid sterility and incompatibility loci across Drosophila species

candidate_datasets.name: Mouse Genome Informatics (MGI)
candidate_datasets.role: Genetic data on mammalian hybrid sterility loci (such as Prdm9 and X-linked incompatibility loci in Mus)

obstacles: While the supernatural 'special endowment' rival is not an empirical hypothesis, the scientific rival (that natural selection directly favors intrinsic hybrid sterility to keep species distinct, i.e., reinforcement of postzygotic sterility) is directly testable by comparing allopatric vs. sympatric patterns and molecular evolution of Dobzhansky-Muller loci.
rationale: Darwin's claim that intrinsic hybrid sterility is an incidental byproduct of independent divergence in reproductive systems rather than an adaptation selected to prevent interbreeding maps directly onto the Dobzhansky-Muller incompatibility model versus postzygotic reinforcement. Comparative allopatric/sympatric crossing data on Dryad and molecular genetics in FlyBase and MGI clearly resolve this in favor of incidental epistatic incompatibility.

operationalization: Across interspecific first crosses in birds (galliforms and passerines) and angiosperms that produce few or no viable offspring, partition failure rates between lack of fertilization versus post-fertilization embryonic arrest/seed abortion (e.g., endosperm failure in seeds, early blastoderm/embryo death in bird eggs).

candidate_datasets.name: Dryad Digital Repository
candidate_datasets.role: Experimental datasets quantifying fertilization rates vs. early embryonic death in interspecific avian crosses and post-fertilization seed abortion (endosperm-embryo incompatibility) in angiosperms

obstacles: Distinguishing unfertilized ova/ovules from very early zygotic death requires microscopic or histological examination of eggs and seeds rather than simple hatching/germination counts.
rationale: Modern studies of reproductive isolation in both birds (including galliforms and estrildid finches) and flowering plants (where post-fertilization endosperm failure and seed abortion are ubiquitous) routinely distinguish pre-fertilization failure from early embryo mortality. Public datasets on Dryad directly confirm that early post-fertilization embryo death accounts for a high proportion of apparent first-cross sterility.

operationalization: Compare the physiological, endocrine, and gametogenic phenotypes of captivity-induced reproductive failure in wild species (despite normal somatic health/survival) with those of interspecific hybrids, testing whether both exhibit selective disruption of gametogenesis/gonadal maturation independent of somatic viability, and whether their underlying cellular mechanisms are shared or distinct.

candidate_datasets.name: Dryad Digital Repository
candidate_datasets.role: Comparative datasets on captive reproductive failure and lifespan in zoo animals vs. hybrid sterility phenotypes

candidate_datasets.name: NCBI Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO)
candidate_datasets.role: Transcriptomic profiles of sterile hybrid gonads vs. environmentally stressed or captive gonadal tissues

obstacles: Phenomenologically both captivity and hybridization can cause selective reproductive failure in otherwise healthy adults, but at the proximate mechanistic level captivity-induced sterility is typically neuroendocrine (HPG axis suppression) whereas hybrid sterility is typically genetic/meiotic (chromosomal mispairing or Dobzhansky-Muller incompatibilities).
rationale: Darwin's comparison has two levels: a phenomenological similarity (selective vulnerability of the reproductive system while somatic health remains intact) and a mechanistic analogy. Existing veterinary/zoo and hybrid biology datasets confirm the phenomenological parallel (somatic vigor paired with gonadal failure), while transcriptomic and physiological data show distinct proximate causes, making the claim partially resolvable.

operationalization: Test for a hump-shaped (quadratic) relationship between parental genetic/geographic distance and offspring fitness/fertility (optimal outcrossing distance: inbreeding depression at zero distance, heterosis at intermediate intraspecific distance, and outbreeding depression/sterility at wide interspecific distance), alongside testing whether mild environmental shifts increase growth/fecundity relative to static or extreme environments.

candidate_datasets.name: Dryad Digital Repository
candidate_datasets.role: Experimental datasets testing optimal outcrossing distance (inbreeding depression, heterosis, and outbreeding depression across genetic distances) in plants and animals

obstacles: The crossing half of the claim (optimal outcrossing distance: heterosis from slight crosses, sterility from wide crosses) is cleanly operationalized and well-supported by data, whereas the environmental half ('slight changes in the conditions of life benefit all organic beings') is vague and depends on whether 'slight change' means relief from local resource depletion/pathogens or abiotic perturbation.
rationale: The genetic crossing component of this claim—that crossing slightly differentiated conspecifics increases vigor and fertility (heterosis) while wider crosses reduce fertility (outbreeding depression and hybrid sterility)—is directly testable and resolved by optimal-outcrossing datasets on Dryad. However, because the companion claim that 'slight changes in conditions of life benefit all organic beings' is much harder to operationalize unambiguously across organisms, the compound claim is partially resolvable.

operationalization: Test for the existence of statistically significant prezygotic cross-incompatibility (e.g., gametophytic incompatibility factors such as $Ga1$ in Zea mays) or postzygotic hybrid sterility/lethality among recognized conspecific varieties, ecotypes, or subspecies in plants and animals.

candidate_datasets.name: MaizeGDB
candidate_datasets.role: Genetic and crossing records of maize varieties carrying gametophytic cross-incompatibility loci (Ga1, Tcb1, Ga2) that cause partial or complete sterility between varieties

candidate_datasets.name: Dryad Digital Repository
candidate_datasets.role: Datasets documenting incipient reproductive isolation and partial hybrid sterility between conspecific varieties/ecotypes in plants (Mimulus, Arabidopsis, Oryza) and animals (Mus, Drosophila)

obstacles: As Darwin noted, if taxonomists reclassify any partially sterile varieties as distinct species solely because of their sterility, the test becomes circular; using independent genomic/taxonomic classifications avoids this.
rationale: Darwin's claim that intraspecific varieties are generally fertile when crossed, but with demonstrable exceptions of partial sterility (such as in maize and Verbascum), is directly testable with modern genetic and crossing databases. MaizeGDB documents the exact gametophytic cross-incompatibility factors in maize varieties, and Dryad contains numerous datasets of partial reproductive isolation among conspecific plant and animal varieties.

operationalization: Compare phenotypic variance ($V_P$ or coefficient of variation) of quantitative morphological and life-history traits in F1 hybrids versus F2 (and subsequent recombinant) hybrid generations across plant and animal crosses.

candidate_datasets.name: Dryad Digital Repository
candidate_datasets.role: Quantitative trait locus (QTL) and biometric datasets containing parental, F1, and F2 phenotypic measurements across interspecific and intervarietal plant and animal crosses

candidate_datasets.name: Germplasm Resources Information Network (GRIN)
candidate_datasets.role: Phenotypic trait records across F1 hybrids and segregating F2 populations in crop species

obstacles: Darwin attributed F2 variability to a vaguely 'disturbed reproductive system', whereas modern genetics explains the exact same empirical pattern via Mendelian segregation, recombination, and transgressive segregation.
rationale: The empirical core of this claim—that F1 hybrids are phenotypically uniform while F2 and later hybrid generations exhibit vastly increased phenotypic variance (including transgressive segregation)—is a foundational law of genetics tested in thousands of QTL and breeding datasets. Public datasets on Dryad containing P1, P2, F1, and F2 trait measurements allow an immediate, decisive test.

operationalization: Compare non-fertility genetic architecture metrics—dominance ratios ('prepotency'), F2 segregation variance, frequency of ancestral trait reappearance ('reversion' via complementary epistasis), and parental phenotypic intermediacy—between interspecific hybrid crosses and intraspecific varietal ('mongrel') crosses across plant and animal QTL datasets.

candidate_datasets.name: Dryad Digital Repository
candidate_datasets.role: Comparative QTL and biometric crossing datasets for both intraspecific (ecotype/variety) and interspecific crosses in plants and animals (e.g., Helianthus, Mimulus, Solanum, Mus, Gasterosteus)

obstacles: Extreme interspecific crosses can show higher rates of segregation distortion and transgressive segregation than close varietal crosses, though both follow the same continuous Mendelian and quantitative genetic rules.
rationale: Darwin's four non-fertility properties—F1/F2 variability, prepotency (dominance), reversion (epistatic complementation of ancestral characters), and parental resemblance—all map onto standard quantitative genetic parameters measured in experimental crosses. Public QTL and biometric datasets on Dryad spanning intraspecific ecotypes and interspecific hybrids confirm that inheritance follows the same quantitative rules across both.

operationalization: Test whether reproductive isolation and genetic divergence across populations, varieties, subspecies, and species form a continuous distribution ('speciation continuum') rather than two discrete, non-overlapping modes separated by an absolute discontinuity in crossability or hybrid fertility.

candidate_datasets.name: Dryad Digital Repository
candidate_datasets.role: Multi-clade speciation continuum datasets measuring reproductive isolation and genomic divergence ($F_{ST}$, $d_{XY}$) across populations, varieties/ecotypes, and species (e.g., Roux et al. 2016 and Coyne & Orr compilations)

obstacles: While framed as a conceptual summary of Chapter VIII, the rival 19th-century hypothesis (that species and varieties are separated by an absolute, qualitative chasm in hybrid sterility) makes a clear empirical prediction that is directly refuted by the continuous distribution of reproductive isolation.
rationale: Although stated as a conceptual conclusion to Chapter VIII, it directly pits the 'speciation continuum' hypothesis against the rival claim of a discrete qualitative boundary in interfertility between varieties and species. Large comparative datasets of reproductive isolation and genomic divergence across populations, varieties, and species on Dryad demonstrate a continuous gradation.

operationalization: In morphological character spaces (PCA or phylogenetic morphospaces) combining extant clades (e.g., Equus vs. Tapirus, or pigeons) and their stem fossils, test whether reconstructed common ancestors and stem fossils lie at ancestral nodes exhibiting mosaic/plesiomorphic character combinations rather than on the direct Euclidean line segment connecting two extant crown species.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoBank
candidate_datasets.role: Total-evidence morphological character matrices containing both extant crown species and extinct stem fossils across vertebrate and invertebrate clades

candidate_datasets.name: Paleobiology Database
candidate_datasets.role: Stratigraphic and taxonomic data on extinct stem taxa (e.g., basal perissodactyls, stem birds, stem cetaceans)

obstacles: Morphospace geometry depends on character selection and scaling, though discrete character polarity (plesiomorphy vs. synapomorphy) unambiguously distinguishes stem progenitors from direct crown-to-crown intermediates.
rationale: Darwin's prediction—that extinct transitional forms connect extant species downward to a shared ancestral progenitor (which differs from all its modified descendants) rather than lying directly between two extant crown species—is the foundation of modern cladistics and phylomorphospace analysis. Morphological matrices in MorphoBank combining fossil stem taxa and extant crown species directly confirm this.

operationalization: Estimate the total cumulative number of extinct species and variety-level lineage segments across the history of life using fossil origination/extinction rates, preservation probability models, and coalescent/diversification models on time-calibrated phylogenies.

candidate_datasets.name: Paleobiology Database
candidate_datasets.role: Global fossil occurrence records for estimating species durations, turnover rates, and preservation probabilities

candidate_datasets.name: TimeTree
candidate_datasets.role: Time-calibrated divergence dates across extant classes and phyla

obstacles: Incongruent precision: 'inconceivably great' is qualitative rather than a specific numerical threshold, and the vast majority of transient variety-level populations leave no direct fossil trace and must be extrapolated from diversification models.
rationale: Paleobiological diversification and preservation models applied to the Paleobiology Database and TimeTree clearly indicate that billions of species and far more variety-level transitional populations have existed over Earth history, vastly outnumbering extant species. However, because variety-level transitional links cannot be directly counted in the fossil record and 'inconceivably great' is qualitative, it is partially resolvable.

operationalization: Compare Darwin's 300-million-year estimate for the time elapsed since the late Cretaceous (Chalk) and the denudation of the Weald against absolute radiometric geochronology of the Cretaceous-Paleogene boundary (66.0 Ma) and thermochronological/geomorphological dating of Wealden uplift and subaerial fluvial erosion.

candidate_datasets.name: International Chronostratigraphic Chart (ICS)
candidate_datasets.role: Global radiometrically calibrated ages of the Upper Cretaceous (Chalk, 100.5–66.0 Ma) and Cenozoic eras

candidate_datasets.name: Macrostrat
candidate_datasets.role: Chronostratigraphic and lithological data for Cretaceous and Cenozoic formations

candidate_datasets.name: British Geological Survey (BGS) Lexicon of Named Rock Units
candidate_datasets.role: Stratigraphic ages, thicknesses, and depositional/erosional history of the Chalk Group and Wealden Group in south-east England

obstacles: None; radiometric dating and modern geomorphology directly and precisely resolve both the age of the Chalk and the mechanism/rate of Wealden denudation.
rationale: Darwin made a concrete quantitative historical inference (~300 million years since the latter part of the Secondary/Cretaceous period based on marine cliff-retreat denudation of the Weald) that he himself later retracted in the 3rd edition. Modern radiometric geochronology (ICS chart: late Cretaceous ended 66 Ma, with Wealden Cenozoic subaerial erosion occurring over ~30–60 Myr) refutes Darwin's 300-Myr figure and his marine-cliff erosion assumption with complete precision.

operationalization: Compare the proportion of wholly soft-bodied vs. biomineralized/skeletal marine taxa in extant marine biodiversity inventories (WoRMS/OBIS) against their representation in the global fossil record (Paleobiology Database), and evaluate taphonomic shell/bone decay rates on non-aggrading seafloors.

candidate_datasets.name: Paleobiology Database
candidate_datasets.role: Global fossil occurrence data categorized by preservation mode (biomineralized vs. exceptional Konservat-Lagerstätten soft-tissue preservation)

candidate_datasets.name: World Register of Marine Species (WoRMS)
candidate_datasets.role: Census of extant marine species across soft-bodied and skeletal phyla to quantify preservation bias

candidate_datasets.name: Dryad Digital Repository
candidate_datasets.role: Live-dead fidelity and experimental marine taphonomy datasets measuring shell/bone dissolution and decay vs. sedimentation rate

obstacles: Taken literally, 'No organism wholly soft can be preserved' is slightly overstated because rare Konservat-Lagerstätten (e.g., Burgess Shale, Chengjiang, Mazon Creek) do preserve soft-bodied organisms, though in normal marine deposits soft-bodied preservation is near zero.
rationale: Both Darwin's strict literal statement ('No organism wholly soft can be preserved') and his broader empirical generalization (that soft-bodied organisms and unburied skeletal remains on non-depositing seafloors rarely survive, creating severe taphonomic bias) can be directly tested today using the Paleobiology Database, WoRMS, and live-dead taphonomic datasets on Dryad.

operationalization: Calculate the distribution of hiatus durations (unconformities separating successive lithostratigraphic units) and completeness fractions across regional and continental sedimentary columns in quantitative chronostratigraphic databases.

candidate_datasets.name: Macrostrat
candidate_datasets.role: Gap-bound chronostratigraphic columns quantifying deposited rock durations vs. unrecorded hiatus intervals between formations

candidate_datasets.name: Paleobiology Database
candidate_datasets.role: Stratigraphic occurrence intervals and temporal gaps across fossiliferous formations

obstacles: Macrostrat's deepest package-level coverage is strongest in North America, the Caribbean, New Zealand, and deep-sea cores, though global compilations and Sadler completeness datasets confirm the pattern worldwide.
rationale: Modern quantitative stratigraphy (such as the Macrostrat database and Sadler completeness analyses) explicitly represents the sedimentary record as gap-bound packages separated by unconformities of measured temporal duration. These open datasets directly confirm that unrecorded hiatus intervals represent the majority of elapsed geological time at any given locality.

operationalization: Test across geological columns whether thick, laterally extensive, richly fossiliferous shallow-marine formations occur predominantly in basins undergoing tectonic/thermal subsidence where accommodation space creation matches sediment supply, by cross-referencing formation thickness, paleobathymetry/facies, and fossil richness.

candidate_datasets.name: Macrostrat
candidate_datasets.role: Unit thickness, areal extent, depositional environment (shallow marine), and tectonic/subsidence setting across thousands of sedimentary formations

candidate_datasets.name: Paleobiology Database
candidate_datasets.role: Fossil occurrence density and diversity linked directly to Macrostrat geological units

obstacles: Eustatic sea-level rise can also create shallow-marine accommodation space over shorter timescales, though accumulating *thick* (hundreds to thousands of meters) shallow-marine sequences that survive subsequent erosion requires crustal subsidence.
rationale: Darwin's insight—that accumulating thick shallow-water fossiliferous formations requires crustal subsidence balanced by sediment supply (what modern sequence stratigraphy calls accommodation space)—is directly testable using the linked Macrostrat and Paleobiology Database records. Comparing unit thickness, shallow-marine facies, and fossil richness confirms this mechanism.

operationalization: Compare marine and island/coastal origination vs. extinction rates and sedimentary rock/fossil accumulation across transgressive (subsidence/relative sea-level rise) vs. regressive (elevation/relative sea-level fall) intervals using coupled paleobiological and stratigraphic datasets, as well as molecular divergence dates of island radiations during emergence vs. submergence.

candidate_datasets.name: Macrostrat
candidate_datasets.role: Sedimentary rock volume, marine flooding area, and hiatus distribution across transgressive and regressive regimes

candidate_datasets.name: Paleobiology Database
candidate_datasets.role: Taxonomic origination and extinction rates across sequence-stratigraphic and sea-level intervals

obstacles: As Darwin himself argues, if periods of elevation leave very little sedimentary record, fossil data alone suffer from severe sampling bias (the Peters/Raup rock-availability effect) during elevation intervals.

In shallow epicontinental seas, marine transgression (subsidence/flooding) often expands habitat area and promotes marine origination (contrary to Darwin's claim for island elevation, where emergence creates isolated archipelagos for terrestrial/littoral speciation).
rationale: Joint analyses of Macrostrat and the Paleobiology Database directly test how sedimentary rock accumulation and fossil preservation covary with subsidence/transgression vs. uplift/regression, and show how unconformities obscure origination events. However, disentangling true origination rates during erosional uplift intervals from rock-volume sampling bias is inherently confounded, making the claim partially resolvable.

operationalization: Compare the empirical distribution of single geological formation durations (in Myr, from Macrostrat) against the empirical distribution of fossil species durations / waiting times to speciation (in Myr, from the Paleobiology Database and TimeTree).

candidate_datasets.name: Macrostrat
candidate_datasets.role: Age bounds and temporal durations (in millions of years) of individual lithostratigraphic formations

candidate_datasets.name: Paleobiology Database
candidate_datasets.role: First and last appearance datums to estimate species durations and turnover timescales across marine clades

candidate_datasets.name: TimeTree
candidate_datasets.role: Molecular divergence times between sister species across animal and plant clades

obstacles: Whether a formation is shorter or longer than a species transition depends on the taxonomic group (e.g., mammal species turn over faster than bivalve species) and how broadly a 'formation' is defined stratigraphically.
rationale: Darwin's hypothesis compares two directly measurable timescales: the temporal duration of a single geological formation and the duration required for species turnover/speciation. Both distributions are openly available in Macrostrat (where formations typically span ~1–5 Myr, often matching or slightly shorter than marine invertebrate species durations of ~2–10 Myr) and the Paleobiology Database, allowing a direct quantitative test.

operationalization: For marine fossil species whose local first appearance occurs mid-formation in a regional basin, test whether earlier fossil occurrences of the same species (or its immediate sister/ancestral population) exist in other geographic basins globally in the Paleobiology Database, indicating regional immigration (range expansion/environmental tracking) rather than in-situ origination.

candidate_datasets.name: Paleobiology Database
candidate_datasets.role: Spatiotemporally resolved global vs. regional first appearance datums (FADs) of marine fossil species across formations

candidate_datasets.name: Macrostrat
candidate_datasets.role: Stratigraphic position and facies shifts within regional formations corresponding to local species appearances

obstacles: Incomplete sampling outside well-studied basins (North America and Europe) can cause a global first appearance to be missed if the species originated in an under-sampled region, though comparing local FADs across multiple well-sampled basins directly measures diachrony and immigration.
rationale: In paleobiology and biostratigraphy, comparing a species' local first appearance datum (local FAD) within a formation against its global first appearance across other basins directly tests whether sudden mid-formation appearances reflect regional immigration/facies tracking rather than in-situ speciation. The Paleobiology Database and Macrostrat provide the exact spatiotemporal occurrence data needed to resolve this.
